utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As I think you've all been told, the Court cannot sit today in the normal way. Judge Robinson being absent on duties elsewhere, and thus not being able to attend today. It was proposed that Judge Bennouna and I would sit under the Rule which allows two Judges to sit but, in fact, over the weekend, he was called away suddenly because of a family illness and so cannot be present today. The position is that it's anticipated that both Judges will be back tomorrow so we can sit then but it does mean, of course, that we can have no hearing of evidence today or no motions hearing. But it occurred to me that it may be convenient to deal with various housekeeping matters and at least the programme for this week and also, as far as possible, to start considering the programme for the autumn. Unless anybody wants to raise anything, it seems to me that the matters we can usefully discuss are these: The programme for the Cerkez Defence witnesses this week, the outstanding motions. There are three Defence motions outstanding and a Prosecution motion, and the affidavits. Those matters must be attended to this week and time must be made available for them. The Cerkez preparations for the autumn, the Prosecution preparations in terms of rebuttal evidence, if there is anything that can be told, and two other matters which have yet to be finalised and those concern the exhibits from the last Kordic witness who was Witness DL, and I think at some stage, we have not yet finalised which exhibits were admitted and which weren't. We need at least to look at that and see what needs to be decided. And also when the Prosecution propose to recall the witness for the tape, Mr. Husic. Generally, if there is any further information on the Kordic exhibits, what progress is being made in their being admitted. So with those matters in mind, we'll begin with the witnesses for Mr. Cerkez. Yes, now, Major Stipo Ceko was giving evidence. He had finished his evidence in chief and was to be cross-examined. Do you know how long that's likely to be, have you any information?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have no idea, Your Honour, how long the Prosecution will need for cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's unlikely to be less than half a day. These witnesses cover the whole territory of Cerkez's Defence and the only way I can reduce the time taken with one witness is forecasting that some of the other topics that I might raise with Witness X it will be possible to put with Witness Y which is what I, by and large, have been doing, but I don't think I will be less than half a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We have your list, Mr. Kovacic. You have four witnesses listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cickovic, is that his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Cickovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We now have his summary, four pages. I don't anticipate he will be one of the longest witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: An hour or so in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We believe that in chief could be between half an hour and one hour. One hour, let's say, maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So it may be possible to get through his evidence or most of it on Tuesday with possibly cross-examination Wednesday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, are the other three witnesses available?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The only issue is all of them are here except the witness under number five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We obviously don't have the same list. I've got one with only four on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I will let you know then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. So Mr. Mlakic, Mr. Jukic and Mr. Kapor are all here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There is a small exchange. Instead of Mr. Kapor, who was not able to go to passport, and I was only informed about that only shortly before the weekend, so he is out for time being. Probably he will be coming in September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got somebody instead of him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We have Ms. Anastasia Protz. We did send a letter to other parties but, unfortunately, obviously the copy was not distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've got it. It's arrived just this moment. So Mr. Mlakic we will call to us, and you've got -- sorry, Mr. Mlakic. Yes, how long is Mr. Mlakic to be, do you anticipate?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: For direct examination, I don't anticipate more than 15, 20 minutes at most. It's practically only on one fact and we are not interested in anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The fact is the position of Mr. Lujic, Lujic Marko, and the recently Mr. Puljic testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I have it. Yes, the artillery point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But it was divided in time. Puljic covered one part in time, this one is supposed to cover the time before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So he, anyway, will not be long. And I now have the new list. Mr. Cickovic we've mentioned. Mr. Zoran Jukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zoran Jukic is a little bit longer, but I don't anticipate more for direct examination, don't anticipate more than one hour let's say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mrs. Protz.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: She will take, for direct examination, not more than 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What does she deal with?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: She is recorded as a witness in the incident murder in hotel, in May 20, 1992. She is recorded as on-site report of investigative judge as witness. So we have located her based on that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the Trako murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. Trako murder in the hotel May 20, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Again, relatively short.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very much so, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we could allow something like six hours for those four witnesses. We may be able to finish those by Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I entirely agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thursday lunchtime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Originally, without anticipating that we will -- not hearing the witnesses this day, we were just about to inform you that according to our expectations, we may be finished -- we may be out of witnesses, better to say, even on Wednesday, late afternoon. So probably now it is Thursday afternoon, as you put it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, very well. That, then, would be convenient, because we could deal with the motions and other matters on Friday morning. Yes. Well, we'll turn to those next. The motions that we have to deal with -- there are three Defence motions filed on the 19th of July. They are for the exclusion of various testimony and to require certification. It would obviously be convenient to deal with all three of those together, and what we'll do is hear them at the end of the evidence. There is also a Prosecution motion, a confidential motion, filed on the 26th of July. Mr. Nice, that's presumably a fairly urgent matter. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it should be addressed as soon as possible. Sometime this week would be sufficient. Depending on the attitude of the Defence to the issue, it may or may not take some time. It could easily go very quickly, because what is, as you will see, I think, proposed is -- well, it could go very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I turn to the Defence on that matter. Mr. Naumovski, clearly if this matter can be resolved this week, then so much the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're quite ready for it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know if you want to put anything in writing or not. Do you propose to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought -- I realised -- I talked with Mr. Sayers, and I do not think we should do that in writing. But he will be back here tomorrow and then we shall decide finally. You know that our attitude is, so perhaps we could only add something regarding the specific proposals, even though we already discussed that subject earlier, as I have just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, I don't know what your attitude is towards it. It may not be appropriate to discuss it today, since I'm sitting alone, but it may be that we can raise it when Mr. Sayers comes back. If you're in favour of the proposal, then perhaps you could mention it to Mr. Nice so arrangements could be made; if you're against it, then of course we'll hear the argument. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, the suggestion is we deal with the matter this week. Are you ready to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, we agree to that, Your Honour. I only, if I may put a reserve, we are not in the position to put anything in writing in this point of time. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. No requirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We could make a note --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No requirements on anybody to put anything in writing. Much better we deal with things orally if we can. The other matter is the affidavits. I'll make sure that I have the affidavits. Mr. Kovacic, there's an affidavit of Ruzica Ceko and another affidavit of Mr. Jakovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Jankovic. It's spelled wrong. Those are the two which you've put forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And then we'll deal with those this week too when we've dealt with the motions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The outstanding matters which I mentioned were, first of all, Witness DL. As I recollect the position, at the end of -- or during his evidence there was a lot of exhibits, I think, that the Prosecution wanted to put in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The position is our evidence was shortened -- our cross-examination was shortened, I having already provided a skeleton argument of the matters on which I wished to cross-examine. Notwithstanding the decision of the Court to allow no further cross-examination, I cannot believe that the documents that I was seeking to put in, or the topics I was cross-examining to or seeking to cross-examine to, were other than relevant, given, for example, that they covered such topics as the targeting of civilian targets and matters of that sort. And so we would seek, I think, all the exhibits that were listed, I think, to go in, and I can support our position in argument on Friday. I'm afraid I haven't brought the list or the documents with me today, although I can get them from my room if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can't deal with it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, would you be prepared to deal, please, with the Witness DL exhibits on Friday or Thursday, whenever we get to it, and let us know what the position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. It might be convenient, Mr. Nice, if you would provide a bundle for the Court, if it hasn't been done, a separate bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you've only had the skeleton argument, and I'll re-serve the skeleton argument and associate the documents with the points identified as right for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- as we argued, right for cross-examination, but in any case, right for dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So if you would produce all the documents in the usual way for us. It may be convenient next to deal with -- unless there's anything else that anybody wants to raise about this week. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, only one thing. Perhaps it is a good time. I don't think that it requires a formal decision of the Chamber, but it does require understanding, I guess. In a way we -- I mean the Cerkez Defence -- made one mistake, or error, better to say. Witness Sajevic warned us while we debriefed him after the testimony that it was very difficult for him to publicly state it about the troops who were involved in Ahmici, and that is because he intends to live there after the testimony in Bosnia with his family, and there are still some extremists who are not very happy when some forces are mentioned. Based on what we learned from that, we would ask Your Honours, whenever we are driving at the part of the testimony where an answer could mean an explicit nomination of certain troops of HVO, we would ask for a closed or private conference. And I would also kindly ask the Prosecution to cooperate on that matter, and when they know they are going to ask a witness about such units, it would be better if it is closed. Otherwise the witnesses are put in a very difficult position. They are simply afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kovacic, if a time comes when you think that a witness is or is likely to be put in fear or might be afraid, then it's always open to you to raise the matter if nobody else does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It is completely clear, Your Honour. I just wanted to use the opportunity to put on the table that we are now much more careful in that. That is, we never ask for specific protective measures or protected witnesses, but now we see that probably there is something as a step in between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I possibly be heard on that just so that I can express my provisional views?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, I think it would be wrong, totally wrong, for there to be any general rule whereby evidence about such a central issue as who committed the atrocities at Ahmici should be given in closed session. Quite wrong. Witnesses come here to give evidence, to give the truth and the whole truth, and they are frankly obliged to answer questions about all topics, sensitive or otherwise. Although if they, the witness, rather than counsel on their behalf, if they, the witness, say that it's going to be difficult for them to answer something publicly, why then, arrangements may be made on a case-by-case basis. I would respectfully suggest that the appropriate course would be for there to be no interruption by the Defence on such topics, but I will -- if I get a negative answer from a witness and if it looks as possible that the witness may be embarrassed or frightened of giving an answer, I can always ask him if he would prefer to reconsider the matter with protective measures. I think it would be quite wrong to say that the public isn't entitled to hear from the Cerkez Defence witnesses open questions inviting open answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, there has been in this trial an ongoing difficulty about witnesses not giving evidence in open session. And Mr. Nice, of the 114 witnesses you called, I cannot now give you the number, but I would have thought getting on for 40 per cent gave evidence with protective measures. Now, there has to be some degree of equality here. If a witness is prepared to give evidence without protective measures, but feels there are matters which are sensitive and that are liable to place him or may be liable to place him in jeopardy, he must be entitled to ask for a private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On a case-by-case basis. I'm not disagreeing with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to make any ruling today, and I'm not seeking to do so, because I think a general ruling would be wrong. But it seems to me that it's open to the witness to ask for a part of his evidence to be given in private session, because inevitably the witness is not going to be as aware of our procedures as those of us who are in Court. Of course, it's possible for you to do it, but it seems equally that it would be wrong to say that the Defence cannot raise the matter if they think it right to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the other thing that concerns me about what Mr. Kovacic says is it would appear about what he says was debriefing that the witness concerned may have been acknowledging that he didn't, in the event, tell us the full content of his memory or give us the full content of his memory. That would be unfortunate of course. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That must be a matter for Mr. Kovacic to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I shan't --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I complete? In answer to Your Honour's general observation about equality and so on, of course I agree with it in a very broad principle, but I think it's also, if I may say so, important to have in mind the difference between the type of witnesses that are being called for the Prosecution and to explain why there was a large number who sought protective measures. They were, for the most part, victims or associates of victims or of -- for those particular municipalities, those who were in the position of victims, and it's hardly surprising and, indeed, it fits, I think, with the practice of the Tribunal generally that those are the people who were seeking protective measures. It has to be remembered that these witnesses, for the most part of the Defence, are not coming along to describe themselves in the position as victims. They are coming along to say that nothing wrong was done or nothing wrong of any significance was done at all and that indeed people are innocent. Now, it's very hard to understand generally why there should be risk on people giving such evidence if giving evidence such honestly, and that leads to my concern, on behalf of the Prosecution, about the notion that there has to be, as it were, some kind of general equality. Yes, of course, on a witness by witness basis, we must be sensitive and I would be, to concerns that they might have about their security. But I don't think, if I may respectfully say so, it's necessarily the case one simply because X witnesses in the Prosecution had some kind of protective measure that there is, as it were, a parallel expectation or similar expectation for a need for the protection for Defence witness. So that's really reinforcing the point I made earlier that I'd invite the Court to deal with it on a case-by-case basis and as it arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, I am not saying there has to be an absolute equality in numbers. The matter is dealt with on a case-by-case basis as we've dealt with it so far. What there has to be is an equality of principle. Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just in order to avoid any misunderstanding, the example I mentioned the witness clearly stated what he asked, I checked the transcripts. So it is not that he avoided the answer. However, there are two things. First, he was little bit reluctant on that part, that is at least -- that was, at least, my impression. And then I ask him during debriefing, and I think this is good example, he told me that it is quite difficult for the witness coming from Bosnia to clearly nominate or identify some parties here publicly because when he would return, there might be reactions, that is all. So it is not -- I am not implying that this witness did not say what he was supposed to say, he did. It is in the transcript. I am just using that opportunity to try everybody to understand in this courtroom that those witnesses are coming from real life. We are trying to avoid closed sessions, and we are trying to avoid nonpublic hearings. I am a very conservative lawyer in that, and I would always like to have open witnesses, and I hope that we will be able to run our case without closed witnesses or pseudonym or whatever. But from time to time, we will ask that some parts of the sessions will be closed. And that is all. There is no need to make any big argument out of that or any big legal philosophy. The issue is relatively simple. As Your Honour noticed, it's a matter of balance. So if we are talking about balance, we have a huge reserve and I don't see, really, any serious problem. I just wanted you to understand that there are some other issues that we, as the lawyers in the courtrooms are, unfortunately, sometimes we neglect to see them. That is all. Very simple. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, unless there's anything else about this week, we'll go on to consider hearings for the autumn. And really, the ball is in your court, Mr. Kovacic. Can you tell us what you propose?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. As I said earlier, we will reorganise ourselves during August because there were some new issues in the Defence and we had to change many things. However, I think that for all practical aspects, of course, the main issue is time, some time frame in which the Court will expect us to present our case. At this point of time, I am quite confident that we will be capable and that we are ready to present our case in -- I'm talking now about September time, about four to five weeks. So time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for one matter and it's this: That there has been a change in the time table, not a significant one, but one involving two days, two or three days at the end of September. Have you got -- have you had a copy of the new calendar?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We saw that, and I don't think that that could tremendously change the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I wonder if I could ask for one, if one's available, please. Thank you very much. Yes, it's that we'll not be sitting on the 2nd of October or the morning of the 3rd of October. I think that's really the only significant change. And there's a Plenary being arranged for one afternoon in September and I think on the 15th of September, if my recollection is right, we are sitting in another case. Yes, we've got another case to deal with. So there's the loss of about three days in all. But looking at the time which is available, four to five weeks should take you roughly to the middle of October. Would that seem a realistic estimate?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It does seem realistically, very much, Your Honour. Even though we were considering to ask the Chamber to give us one short break sometime in the middle of time given to us for presentation of our evidence, because then probably we will be much more productive or precise in the second part, and then we still could be in the time frame you roughly planned for our Defence. It would help us tremendously in organising a matter and checking, once again, approximately how far the case where are we, did we miss something, et cetera. There is no need to explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So that would be after, roughly, two and a half weeks to three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us look. If you've got the calendar in front of you, we can actually look at the days. I can't make any decisions today, but at least we'll know what your submissions are. [Trial Chamber confers with legal officer]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Looking at the mathematics of it, it appears that by the 28th of September, you will have had 16 days, allowing for half days and this sort of thing, and the days where we are engaged on other matters, that is just slightly over three weeks. There will then be a break because we're not sitting on the Friday, the 29th so in fact it fits in with your submission. We're not sitting on the Monday, October 2nd. We are not sitting at the moment on the morning of the 3rd. No doubt we could accommodate you by taking the afternoon too. If, then, you -- if we did that, that would leave you with -- so you've virtually got a week off. You would then have two and a half weeks in which to conclude your case. Would that accommodate your suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it's not for me to decide by myself, but it seems a sensible solution and we'll let you know on Friday whether we're going to do that. Do you think then -- well, you would effectively have had five and a half weeks which should be ample for you to finish your case if what you say is accurate which I have no doubt it is. And then we would aim to finish your case by the 20th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is our plan and, of course, I cannot tell you now 100 per cent but we are doing -- we are trying, indeed, to organise our Defence in a way to do that within that time, and I'm sure that we will be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. You will obviously provide summaries of those witnesses who are going to give evidence in September as soon as possible and certainly a fortnight before the hearing. Are you in a position to tell us how many, roughly, witnesses, you think you might now be calling?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would not like, Your Honour, to commit myself too much on numbers because we see that a certain number of witnesses will be introduced through the affidavits. And that is, indeed, the main thing we are doing in restructuring the list. We will be able to do that during the recess, as you said, at least 14 days before we started. So we will file revised list of the witnesses and, of course, we are not still sure which witnesses we may use in the form of introduction of the transcripts from other cases. There are some which obviously could save us two or three witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The sooner, if I might say, you get that in hand, the better. If you can do that after the recess so that we have the opportunity to consider it. This is the transcript witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean during September or today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, no, not today. But if, during the recess, you could get in hand the transcript witnesses that you want so that we can consider it at a fairly early stage and you, if necessary, can call the witnesses if the transcripts are not admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Surely. We will try to do that on the very early phase of September case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Do you think on that time table, because I'm going to turn to the Prosecution next, there is a chance that you might finish your case before the 20th of October so that if necessary, we could start calling -- or the Prosecution could start calling their rebuttal case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this phase, it is really difficult to say, and I wouldn't like to be committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But there is a chance. I really cannot tell you how high or how low. Of course, as soon as we see how fast we are progressing, then probably we will inform the other party as soon as we make any judgement, forecast. But I'm a little bit afraid that it will be a little bit too early to tell anything more specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything else you want to raise, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I did plan for this morning, but now we are not in session, but just for your information, Your Honour, we would like to raise also a question which we mentioned once just shortly, but now I started it and I would like to argue on that, appearance of Mr. Blaskic as a witness in our case on -- just on a very brief limited fact. I would ask the Court to establish the rules for that so we can talk to Blaskic Defence counsel and see whether they will comply. It is -- I will not argue that, of course, now, but it is very important for us related to the planning of the witnesses, because it's one fact which could very easily be confirmed by Blaskic and very complicated, if not impossible, if we are trying to prove that indirectly by some other stories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you discussed this with the lawyers for Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I did not discuss that yet with Kordic. I discussed it briefly with Blaskic lawyers. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one matter. It may be helpful if you talked to both Mr. Naumovski about this, and also the Prosecution, to see if there can be some measure of agreement about it. I'm not sure it's a matter which the Trial Chamber has to rule on, but we would hear argument. There's something I'm going to ask the legal officer. [Trial Chamber confers with legal officer]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I've had a word with the legal officer and it may be helpful if you spoke to her. It may be possible to -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Certainly I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- agree something. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: (redacted). So I'd prefer to see that in writing, if Mr. Kovacic is able to assist, but I'll discuss it with him today, of course. As to the position of the Cerkez witnesses, we would very much like and would be assisted by a list of the witnesses that the Cerkez Defence intends to call and we'd like that list as soon as possible, without prejudice to the fact that some of them may not turn up. We quite understand that listed witnesses can't necessarily all attend, or don't necessarily all attend, but our preparation is made very much easier by advance notice, for two reasons: One, because you can prepare the witnesses or prepare for the witnesses; and two, because we can then more helpfully partition up the material to be put in cross-examination between witnesses who we know, or at least reasonably expect to be coming, as opposed to having to try and put it all to the same witness. I remind the Chamber again that the Prosecution gave six weeks' witness lists and more; indeed, in November of last year gave a final list effectively for all witnesses until April. So I would ask Mr. Kovacic to give us a list as soon as may be and not simply wait until two weeks before the sitting days, especially since in the summer most members of the team will be away, for some or most of the time, from The Hague. On the question of the timetable, obviously if there is any time in October to call rebuttal evidence, we will do our very best to have rebuttal evidence available to be called then. Before I come to that, though, I should cautiously remind the Chamber that there were a couple of witnesses intended to be called by the Chamber itself that were going to take some time. There are witnesses, like the tape witness, to be recalled as part of the Prosecution's case, effectively. No question of them being rebuttal witnesses. In particular, the tape witness has to be recalled because he wasn't fully and properly cross-examined at the time. We haven't yet discovered his availability for September. We did discover that he wasn't available for any of the time up and until the end of these sittings. And in any event, it didn't look very likely that we would be able to accommodate him, given the full Cerkez timetable. But those witnesses also do have to be accommodated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. But the tape witness, I should have thought, could well be interposed at a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. As soon as we can find a convenient time for him. And of course the Witness AO has to come back as well. That's another witness who the Chamber has ordered should return to give evidence further in light of other documents that were served.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Talking of the Chamber's witnesses, it may be convenient -- again, this is subject to availability -- to look at the week of the 16th of October for them, which would be the very last week of the Cerkez Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But again one would have to see how that works.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I can help, I know the Chamber was going to turn to me about rebuttal evidence. I stand by my earlier promise to notify the Chamber and Defence as soon as I know that I intend to seek to call evidence in rebuttal. I remind Your Honour that I've always expressed concern about the potential for a substantial amount of material needing to be dealt with, both because of the discovery of documents in Zagreb and maybe for other reasons. And very anxious though I am personally to finish this case on the date given, effectively given in this schedule, I, of course, have to reserve my position. The documents, as the Chamber knows, are still being produced at a fairly substantial rate and are being translated as swiftly as the institution's systems allow. We are, I think, particularly with Mr. Kovacic, concerned to ensure that all parties have the same documents coming from this particular source, and I hope we can arrange that that does happen. But nevertheless, it may take some time to produce these documents simply as part of the rebuttal evidence. As to when I'm going to be able to give you and Defence counsel formal notification of what I expect to lead, I can't really put a date on it. I can simply say as soon as I possibly can, in everybody's interest, not least ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers raised last week the possibility of a pre-rebuttal conference. It seems a sensible idea, and that would at least concentrate minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I respectfully suggest that the break in the Cerkez, the timing of the break in the Cerkez case, that five-day period, the beginning or end of that period might be a sensible time. Because if Cerkez is stocktaking then, it might be sensible indeed, I suppose, immediately after the break, if Cerkez is stocktaking and able to give then an estimate of how much of the remaining time will be required, that would be a sensible time or it might be a sensible time for us to give our position as then understood and it would give us a time to work to. So if I understood Your Honour correctly, can I propose that it's when we resume -- assuming that the Chamber of Your Honour and Your Honour's colleagues makes the decision you've hinted at as a possibility, can I suggest that the rebuttal Status Conference is timetabled for the day that we start sitting, which would be, I think, the 4th of October or possibly the 3rd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We shall be sitting again on the 4th if we don't sit on the afternoon of the 3rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be proper to deal with this when the Chamber is fully constituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But that can be added to the list of things to be dealt with on Friday. Speaking for myself, I shall need to consider very carefully the extent and scope of rebuttal evidence, but I shall say no more. It will be a matter for the Trial Chamber to rule. But let's not argue the matter now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have to say, I wouldn't have expected Your Honour to express a different view, and I will be mindful of it. Nevertheless, we shall see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Anything else that anybody wants to raise? Very well. We'll sit again tomorrow at half past 9.00.
